name: Cairo & Giza
tagline: Egypt's sprawling capital, where the last surviving Ancient Wonder of the World still rises from the desert at the city's edge.
highlight: Standing at the base of the Great Pyramid of Giza, unable to fully comprehend that it was already over 2,000 years old when Cleopatra was born.
shortDescription: Egypt's sprawling capital, home to the Great Pyramids of Giza, the Sphinx, and a historic old city of mosques, museums and centuries-old bazaars.
metaDescription: A Cairo and Giza travel guide: the Great Pyramids, the Sphinx, the Grand Egyptian Museum, food and how to plan a visit to Egypt's capital.
knownFor: The Great Pyramids, the Sphinx, ancient Egyptian history
goodFor: Ancient history, museums, an essential first stop

image.alt: The Great Pyramids of Giza on the edge of Cairo

intro: Cairo is one of the world's great sprawling capitals, a city of over 20 million people that has grown right up to the edge of the Giza plateau, where the last surviving Ancient Wonder of the World still stands.
The Great Pyramids are almost impossibly old — already ancient ruins by the time of Cleopatra, built more than 4,500 years ago and still the most recognisable monuments on Earth.

Most visitors spend a few days here at the start of their Egypt trip, splitting time between Giza's pyramids, the treasures of the Grand Egyptian Museum, and the old city's centuries-old mosques and bazaars.

whyVisit.intro: Cairo and Giza's case rests on being the essential, unmissable starting point for any Egypt trip.

points.title: The Great Pyramids are unmissable
points.text: The last surviving Ancient Wonder of the World, and still the most recognisable monument on Earth.

points.title: The Grand Egyptian Museum is a world-class collection
points.text: Housing Tutankhamun's full treasure hoard and thousands of other ancient artefacts.

points.title: Islamic Cairo is a living historic city
points.text: Centuries-old mosques and markets still in daily use, not preserved as a museum piece.

points.title: It's the essential gateway to the rest of Egypt
points.text: Nearly every Egypt itinerary starts or ends in Cairo.

points.title: Khan el-Khalili is one of the world's great bazaars
points.text: A centuries-old market still selling spices, lanterns and crafts to locals and visitors alike.

attractionsIntro: Cairo and Giza's essential sights combine the world's most famous ancient monuments with a living historic old city.

attractions.name: The Great Pyramids of Giza
attractions.text: The last surviving Ancient Wonder of the World, three monumental pyramids built over 4,500 years ago as royal tombs.
attractions.tip: Arrive at opening time to beat both the desert heat and the busiest tour groups.

attractions.name: The Great Sphinx
attractions.text: One of the world's largest and oldest monolithic statues, its lion's body and human face guarding the pyramid complex.
attractions.tip: The classic photo angle, appearing to touch the Sphinx's nose, requires standing at a specific spot your guide can show you.

attractions.name: The Grand Egyptian Museum

image.alt: The Grand Egyptian Museum near Giza

attractions.text: One of the world's largest archaeological museums, housing Tutankhamun's complete treasure collection among thousands of other artefacts.
attractions.tip: Allow a full half-day — the collection is far too extensive to rush.

attractions.name: The Egyptian Museum, Tahrir Square

image.file: File:Facade of the Egyptian Museum, Tahrir Square, Cairo, Egypt1.jpg
image.alt: The Egyptian Museum in Tahrir Square, Cairo

attractions.text: Cairo's original antiquities museum, a beautifully old-fashioned setting still holding significant artefacts.
attractions.tip: Worthwhile even with the Grand Egyptian Museum now open, for a different, more historic display style.

attractions.name: Khan el-Khalili

image.alt: The Khan el-Khalili bazaar in Cairo

attractions.text: A centuries-old bazaar, its narrow lanes packed with spices, lanterns, jewellery and workshops still in daily use.
attractions.tip: Polite bargaining is expected and part of the shopping experience here.

attractions.name: The Cairo Citadel & Mohammed Ali Mosque

image.file: File:The mosque of Mohammed Ali at the Cairo Citadel.jpg
image.alt: The Mohammed Ali Mosque at the Cairo Citadel

attractions.text: A striking Ottoman-style mosque atop a medieval fortress, with sweeping views over the whole city.
attractions.tip: The citadel's elevated position offers one of Cairo's best panoramic views, pyramids included on a clear day.

attractions.name: Sultan Hassan Mosque
attractions.text: One of Cairo's most impressive medieval mosques, a masterpiece of Mamluk architecture dating to the 14th century.
attractions.tip: The mosque's massive scale is best appreciated from its central courtyard.

thingsToDoIntro: Cairo and Giza reward mixing the pyramids with the old city's mosques and bazaars.

thingsToDo.title: Ride a camel around the pyramids

image.file: File:Camel riding at the Giza Pyramids in Egypt.JPG
image.alt: Camel riding at the Giza Pyramids

thingsToDo.text: A classic, if slightly touristy, way to see the pyramids from a desert vantage point.
thingsToDo.tip: Agree the price and duration clearly before mounting — this is a common area for overcharging.

thingsToDo.title: Explore the Grand Egyptian Museum's collection

image.alt: Exhibits inside the Grand Egyptian Museum

thingsToDo.text: An absorbing half-day, taking in thousands of years of ancient Egyptian history and artefacts.
thingsToDo.tip: Book tickets online ahead — the museum's popularity means walk-up queues can be long.

thingsToDo.title: Bargain at Khan el-Khalili

image.file: File:Flickr - HuTect ShOts - Khan El-Khalili Street شارع خان الخليلي - Cairo - Egypt - 09 04 2010.jpg

thingsToDo.text: A lively way to spend an afternoon, browsing spices, textiles and crafts through the bazaar's narrow lanes.
thingsToDo.tip: A small glass of tea at a bazaar café makes a nice break between shopping stops.

thingsToDo.title: Climb the Cairo Citadel

image.file: File:Mohammed Ali Mosque, Citadel interior, Cairo, Egypt, North Africa.jpg
image.alt: Inside the Mohammed Ali Mosque at the Cairo Citadel

thingsToDo.text: A worthwhile half-day, exploring the mosque's ornate interior and the citadel's sweeping city views.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with a visit to the nearby National Military Museum, included within the citadel grounds.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Islamic Cairo's mosques

image.alt: The interior of Sultan Hassan Mosque

thingsToDo.text: A rewarding walk through centuries of Islamic architecture, still functioning as active places of worship.
thingsToDo.tip: Dress modestly and remove shoes before entering any mosque.

thingsToDo.title: View the pyramids from a desert panorama point

image.file: File:Sphinx and pyramids of Giza panorama.jpg
image.alt: A panoramic desert view of the pyramids and Sphinx

thingsToDo.text: An essential photo stop, a slightly elevated desert viewpoint capturing all three pyramids together.
thingsToDo.tip: Visit in late afternoon for the warmest, most flattering light on the stone.

foodIntro: Cairo's food represents Egyptian cuisine at its best, from humble street stalls to more refined restaurants.

foods.name: Koshari

image.alt: Koshari, Egypt's national dish of rice, lentils and pasta

foods.text: Egypt's national dish, found at dedicated koshari shops throughout the city at every price point.

foods.name: Ful medames

image.alt: Ful medames, a traditional Egyptian fava bean breakfast

foods.text: An essential Cairo breakfast, slow-cooked fava beans found at street stalls citywide.
foods.whereToTry: Breakfast stalls and cafés throughout Cairo.

foods.name: Grilled kofta

image.alt: Grilled kofta, spiced minced meat skewers

foods.text: A beloved grilled dish, spiced minced meat skewers found across the city's restaurants.

foods.name: Taameya (Egyptian falafel)
foods.text: Egypt's own fava bean version of falafel, a beloved street food found on nearly every corner.

foods.name: Molokhia
foods.text: A beloved home-style dish, a thick green soup found at traditional restaurants across the city.

foods.name: Karkade (hibiscus tea)
foods.text: A refreshing national drink, served hot or cold at cafés throughout the city.

areas.text: Closer to Khan el-Khalili, the Egyptian Museum and Islamic Cairo's mosques.

bestTime.headline: October to April for the mildest, most comfortable temperatures
bestTime.summary: Cairo's desert climate makes winter and shoulder season far more comfortable for a full day of sightseeing at Giza.

seasons.text: The mildest temperatures for a full day of pyramid sightseeing, also the busiest season.
Warm but manageable heat with thinner crowds than peak winter.
Intense heat at the exposed Giza plateau, best managed with an early start.

bestTime.avoid: A midday Giza visit in summer — plan for an early morning start regardless of season.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make a Cairo and Giza stay noticeably smoother.
tips: Book Grand Egyptian Museum tickets online ahead to skip long walk-up queues.
Arrive early at Giza to beat both the heat and the tour bus crowds.
Agree prices upfront for camel rides, taxis and unofficial guides.
Dress modestly when visiting mosques, and carry a scarf for women entering.
Budget extra time for Cairo's traffic between destinations.
Carry small cash for tips, expected throughout your visit.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Cairo and Giza?
faq.a: Three days covers the pyramids, the Grand Egyptian Museum and Islamic Cairo comfortably.

faq.q: Are the pyramids actually in Cairo?
faq.a: On Cairo's western edge, in Giza — technically a separate city that has effectively merged with greater Cairo's sprawl.

faq.q: Is the Grand Egyptian Museum worth visiting alongside the older Egyptian Museum?
faq.a: Yes, both are worthwhile — the Grand Egyptian Museum houses the major Tutankhamun collection, while the older museum offers a different, more historic display style.
Generally yes in main tourist areas, with persistent touting around Giza the main practical nuisance rather than serious danger.

faq.q: How do you avoid pyramid scams?
faq.a: Agree prices upfront for any camel ride, guide or 'special access' offer, and be firm about declining unsolicited assistance.

faq.q: Can you enter the pyramids themselves?
faq.a: Yes, for an additional fee — though the interior chambers are relatively plain compared to the exterior's scale.
